source: Penetrating further and further into the heart of the Japanese cruising ground, the Pequod was soon all astir in the fishery. Often, in mild, pleasant weather, for twelve, fifteen, eighteen, and twenty hours on the stretch, they were engaged in the boats, steadily pulling, or sailing, or paddling after the whales, or for an interlude of sixty or seventy minutes calmly awaiting their uprising; though with but small success for their pains.

At such times, under an abated sun; afloat all day upon smooth, slow heaving swells; seated in his boat, light as a birch canoe; and so sociably mixing with the soft waves themselves, that like hearth-stone cats they purr against the gunwale; these are the times of dreamy quietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliancy of the ocean’s skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it; and would not willingly remember, that this velvet paw but conceals a remorseless fang.

These are the times, when in his whale-boat the rover softly feels a certain filial, confident, land-like feeling towards the sea; that he regards it as so much flowery earth; and the distant ship revealing only the tops of her masts, seems struggling forward, not through high rolling waves, but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie: as when the western emigrants’ horses only show their erected ears, while their hidden bodies widely wade through the amazing verdure.

The long-drawn virgin vales; the mild blue hill-sides; as over these there steals the hush, the hum; you almost swear that play-wearied children lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad May-time, when the flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most mystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate, and form one seamless whole.

Nor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail of at least as temporary an effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem to open in him his own secret golden treasuries, yet did his breath upon them prove but tarnishing.

Oh, grassy glades! oh, ever vernal endless landscapes in the soul; in ye,—though long parched by the dead drought of the earthy life,—in ye, men yet may roll, like young horses in new morning clover; and for some few fleeting moments, feel the cool dew of the life immortal on them. Would to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled, mingling threads of life are woven by warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady unretracing progress in this life; we do not advance through fixed gradations, and at the last one pause:—through infancy’s unconscious spell, boyhood’s thoughtless faith, adolescence’ doubt (the common doom), then scepticism, then disbelief, resting at last in manhood’s pondering repose of If. But once gone through, we trace the round again; and are infants, boys, and men, and Ifs eternally. Where lies the final harbor, whence we unmoor no more? In what rapt ether sails the world, of which the weariest will never weary? Where is the foundling’s father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unwedded mothers die in bearing them: the secret of our paternity lies in their grave, and we must there to learn it.
And that same day, too, gazing far down from his boat’s side into that same golden sea, Starbuck lowly murmured:—

“Loveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride’s eye!—Tell me not of thy teeth-tiered sharks, and thy kidnapping cannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep down and do believe.”
And Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same golden light:—
“I am Stubb, and Stubb has his history; but here Stubb takes oaths that he has always been jolly!”

modern_en.title: Chapter 114 — The Gilder
paragraphs: Pushing deeper and deeper into the heart of the Japanese cruising ground, the Pequod was soon in a constant bustle with the fishery. Often, in mild, pleasant weather, the crew spent twelve, fifteen, eighteen and twenty hours at a stretch in the boats, steadily rowing, sailing or paddling after the whales, or, for a spell of sixty or seventy minutes, waiting calmly for them to surface — though they had little success for all their trouble.

At such times, under a softened sun, afloat all day upon smooth, slow-heaving swells, seated in his boat as light as a birch canoe, and so sociably mingling with the soft waves themselves that, like hearthstone cats, they purr against the gunwale — these are the times of dreamy quietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliance of the ocean's skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it; and would not willingly remember that this velvet paw but conceals a merciless fang.

At such times the wanderer in his whaleboat quietly feels a certain filial, trusting, land-like feeling toward the sea, and looks on it as so much flowery earth. The distant ship, with only the tops of her masts showing, seems to struggle forward not through high rolling waves but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie — the way the western emigrants' horses show only their pricked-up ears while their hidden bodies wade far and wide through the astonishing greenery.

The long-drawn virgin valleys; the mild blue hillsides; as the hush, the hum steals over these, you would almost swear that play-weary children lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad springtime, when the flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most mystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate and form one seamless whole.

Nor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail to have at least an equally temporary effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem to open his own secret golden treasuries within him, his breath upon them proved only tarnishing.

Oh, grassy glades! Oh, endless landscapes of everlasting spring in the soul! In you — though you have long been parched by the dead drought of our earthy life — in you men can still roll like young horses in fresh morning clover, and for a few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of immortal life on them. I wish to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled and mingling threads of life are woven warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady progress in this life that never doubles back; we do not climb through fixed stages and then rest at the last one. We pass through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's unthinking faith, adolescence's doubt (the common fate), then skepticism, then disbelief, and come to rest at last in manhood's brooding repose of If. But once we have gone through it all, we go round the circle again, and are infants, boys and men, and Ifs, forever. Where is the final harbor, from which we will never cast off again? In what ecstatic ether does that world sail — the world that even the weariest will never tire of? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unmarried mothers die giving birth to them: the secret of who our father is lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.
That same day, too, Starbuck, gazing far down from the side of his boat into the same golden sea, murmured quietly:

"Loveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride's eye! Do not tell me of your teeth-tiered sharks and your kidnapping cannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep down and do believe."
And Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same golden light:
"I'm Stubb, and Stubb has a history; but right here Stubb swears that he has always been jolly!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 114 — Forgylderen
paragraphs: Pequod trængte dybere og dybere ind i hjertet af det japanske fangstfelt og havde snart travlt med fiskeriet hele tiden. Ofte, når vejret var mildt og lunt, tilbragte mandskabet tolv, femten, atten og tyve timer i træk i bådene, hvor de roede, sejlede eller padlede jævnt af sted efter hvalerne, eller i en stund på tres eller halvfjerds minutter lå og ventede roligt på, at de skulle dukke op — men trods al deres umage havde de kun ringe held.

På sådanne tider, under en blidere sol, drivende hele dagen på glatte, langsomt hævende dønninger, siddende i sin båd, der er let som en birkekano, og så omgængeligt blandet med de bløde bølger selv, at de som kakkelovnskatte spinder mod essingen — det er tiderne med drømmende stilhed, hvor man, når man ser havets rolige skønhed og glans på dets hud, glemmer tigerhjertet, der pruster dernede under den, og nødig vil huske, at denne fløjlsbløde pote kun skjuler en ubarmhjertig tand.

På sådanne tider føler vandreren i sin hvalbåd stille en vis barnlig, tillidsfuld, landlig følelse over for havet og ser på det som så meget blomstrende jord. Det fjerne skib, hvoraf kun mastetoppene viser sig, synes at kæmpe sig frem, ikke gennem høje, rullende bølger, men gennem det høje græs på en bølgende prærie — ligesom de vestlige nybyggeres heste kun viser deres opspilede ører, mens deres skjulte kroppe vader vidt og bredt gennem det forbløffende grønne.

De langstrakte, jomfruelige dale; de milde, blå bakkesider; når stilheden og summen sniger sig over dem, kunne man næsten sværge på, at legetrætte børn ligger og sover i disse ødemarker, i et glad forår, hvor skovens blomster er plukket. Og alt dette blander sig med din mest mystiske stemning, så virkelighed og fantasi mødes halvvejs, trænger ind i hinanden og danner én sømløs helhed.

Sådanne beroligende syn, hvor midlertidige de end var, undlod heller ikke at have en mindst lige så midlertidig virkning på Ahab. Men selv om disse hemmelige gyldne nøgler syntes at åbne hans egne hemmelige gyldne skatkamre indeni ham, viste hans ånde på dem sig kun at gøre dem matte.

Åh, græsklædte lunde! Åh, endeløse landskaber med evigt forår i sjælen! I jer — selv om I længe har været udtørret af vort jordiske livs døde tørke — i jer kan menneskene endnu rulle sig som unge heste i frisk morgenkløver og i nogle få flygtige øjeblikke føle den kølige dug fra det udødelige liv på sig. Gud give, at disse velsignede vindstille ville vare ved. Men livets sammenblandede og sammenvævede tråde er vævet i skær og islæt: stille krydset af storm, en storm for hver stille. Der er ingen jævn fremgang i dette liv, der aldrig bøjer tilbage; vi klatrer ikke gennem faste trin for til sidst at hvile på det sidste. Vi går gennem barndommens ubevidste fortryllelse, drengeårenes tankeløse tro, ungdommens tvivl (den almindelige skæbne), så skepsis, så vantro, og når til sidst til ro i mandsalderens grublende hvile i Hvis. Men når vi først har været det hele igennem, går vi kredsen rundt igen og er spædbørn, drenge og mænd og Hvis, for evigt. Hvor er den sidste havn, hvorfra vi aldrig mere skal sætte fra land? I hvilken henrykt æter sejler den verden — den verden, som selv den mest trætte aldrig bliver træt af? Hvor er hittebarnets far skjult? Vore sjæle er som de forældreløse, hvis ugifte mødre dør ved at føde dem: hemmeligheden om, hvem vor far er, ligger i deres grav, og vi må derhen for at få den at vide.
Samme dag mumlede Starbuck, der sad og stirrede langt ned over siden af sin båd ned i det samme gyldne hav, stille:

»Uudgrundelig dejlighed, som nogen elsker nogensinde så i sin unge bruds øje! Fortæl mig ikke om jeres tandrækkede hajer og jeres bortfører-kannibalvaner. Lad troen fordrive kendsgerningen; lad fantasien fordrive erindringen; jeg ser dybt ned og tror.«
Og Stubb sprang op som en fisk med glitrende skæl i det samme gyldne lys:
»Jeg er Stubb, og Stubb har en fortid; men lige her sværger Stubb på, at han altid har været glad!«
